utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: This afternoon we have a Status Conference in this case to mainly see how the pre-trial stage is going. I note that the accused are on provisional release, and the Trial Chamber did receive a report from the relevant authorities in their country that compliance with the Trial Chamber's orders has not been a problem with all the three accused. So the position as of now is quite satisfactory. I haven't asked about the parties because I assumed that they are still the same, but I have noticed some new faces. Maybe I can have a formal presentation. The Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Good afternoon, Counsel. For the Prosecution appear Mr. David Re, trial attorney; Mr. George David Hackney, legal officer; Ms. Diana Dicklich, case manager; and myself, Ekkehard Withopf, acting senior trial attorney.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. The Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. Edina Residovic, attorney at law from Sarajevo, counsel for General Enver Hadzihasanovic, together with my co-counsel, my colleague, Stefane Bourgon, an attorney at law from Canada.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Vasvija Vidovic, attorney at law from Sarajevo, together with Mr. John Jones, attorney at law from Great Britain, Defence counsel, together with my co-counsel, for General Mehmed Alagic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. My name is Ibrisimovic, and together with co-counsel, we represent Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. I welcome the new co-counsel, Mr. Stefane Bourgon, to these proceedings. I received a report from the Senior Legal Officer on the discussions that went on during the meeting I think yesterday on the preparations for trial. There are a few things that maybe we can discuss briefly during this Status Conference. I note that the Trial Chamber is still considering some motions which have been filed, one of them dealing with the form of the amended indictment, and the Trial Chamber will be issuing a Scheduling Order soon after the decision has been handed down. We also have matters from the report dealing with disclosure: compliance with Rule 66(A)(ii) and Rule 92 bis, compliance with Rule 66(B), Rule 66(C), and also Rule 67 and Rule 68. I note especially with regard to Rule 92 bis that the Prosecution is going in the right direction, having some Prosecution witness statements recorded. This does definitely help with scheduling the trial. I wanted to find out whether there are any problems at this stage on the disclosure stage with the documents and also with the Sarajevo collection. There appears to be a satisfactory report. Is there anything the Prosecution would like to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: May I first address the issue regarding the submissions regarding challenges to jurisdiction if I'm allowed to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: I understand that you have been comprehensively informed by the Senior Legal Officer about the discussions held yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: It was again a very productive meeting in detail discussing all issues arisen in the past. With regard to the timetable submissions to the challenges to jurisdiction, I would like to make some principal remarks. The decision on the challenge to jurisdiction, in particular regarding the applicability of Article 7(3) in a non-international armed conflict is crucial for the future proceedings in this case. Significant portions, I repeat significant portions of the amended indictment depend on this decision. Logic requires to get a decision on this issue prior to any further movement in this case, and it also can be anticipated that the party whose submission will not be granted will appeal the decision. Realistically, a final decision of the Appeals Chamber cannot be expected prior to late summer 2002, maybe even later. That's reason enough to speed up things and to get the ball rolling. The fact that this issue is pending has a serious impact on the case preparation on the side of the Prosecution in many regards. I want to provide Your Honour only with two significant examples. Following our obligation under Rule 92 bis to speed up proceedings, we are currently planning a mission to take the declarations, to take the Rule 92 bis declarations involving staff of the OTP, involving staff of the Registry, involving national authorities. This causes a lot of expenses, and the Prosecution is reluctant to spend a lot of UN money without knowing whether the underlying relevant portions of the amended indictment will stay. I will provide you with a second example, and this one is as serious as the first one. Currently we are establishing contact to an outside military expert in order to get his assistance as a Prosecution military expert. Again, to hire him causes a lot of expenses that could be completely or to a high percentage a waste of money if the decision of the Trial Chamber or the Appeals Chamber would be against the Prosecution's position. To not have a final decision on this issue has obviously a very practical implication. Therefore, the Prosecution proposed, as you know, 28 days for each party to file, to concurrently file their submissions and ten days for cross-responses. This seems to be reasonable and more realistic than the Defence proposal, 60 days for submission, 6-0 days for submissions for each party and 15 days for cross-responses. The main issue, as you know, is applicability of Article 7(3) on non-international armed conflict. That's an old issue. This issue was first raised by the Defence in their joint preliminary motion on the original indictment. This motion has been filed the 8th of October, 2001. Since then, five and a half months have passed by. The Defence knows since 17th December last year that this issue has to be addressed at least in a pre-trial brief. Again, three months passed. This has been sufficient time for preparation. The Prosecution has used this time. The Prosecution would be in a position to file its submission within 21 days starting from today. The submission should be filed concurrently. That's the position of the Prosecution. Otherwise, there would be further delay in the proceedings and there would be an undue advantage for the Defence if they were allowed to respond to the Prosecution's submission again. Yesterday --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel is kindly requested to slow down, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: I apologise. With regard to the page limits, we yesterday discussed to some length. Obviously ten pages are not sufficient. An agreement has been reached, at least I understand an agreement has been reached amongst the parties that both parties should be allowed to file 50 pages each. I want to stress that if the Defence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Fifty pages, 5-0.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Five zero.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Each.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Each.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Each defendant.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: No. Yeah, each party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Each party.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Each party. However, the Defence, at least yesterday, hadn't made a final decision whether they want to file a joint submission or three separate submissions. If the Defence intends to follow the line of separate submissions, the combination, the combination of these submissions, for obvious reasons, should not exceed fifty, 5-0 pages, meaning each party works under exactly the same page limitation. There's another regard with the challenges to jurisdiction. That is the issue of oral hearing. The Prosecution is of the opinion that an oral hearing is not necessary, considering that this would cause a repetition, only a repetition of the legal arguments exchanged in the submissions of the parties and would again delay proceedings. Last issue in this regard, that's the issue of having amici curiae invited to provide their submissions. That has been a consideration by the Presiding Judge following a proposal by the Defence, a proposal by the Defence to invite the permanent members of the Security Council. The Prosecution does not take a specific position in this regard. However, considers the use of amici curiae a potential reason for again a significant delay in the proceedings. In addition, regarding the permanent members of the Security Council as proposed by the Defence, the intention is only one source amongst others with regard to the interpretation of Article 7(3) and its applicability. We also have to rely on the jurisdiction of the ICTY. The Defence argument, therefore, is not convincing to invite them. If I may summarise the Prosecution's position, things can only speed up by the Trial Chamber. It's up to the Trial Chamber to get the ball rolling. Not having a final decision on the issues involved seriously hampers the further proceedings. Again, I want to stress the Prosecution is ready, is ready to file a submission on short notice, meaning 21 days from today on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. Any response or submissions by the Defence of the first accused?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. I probably got an interpretation that is not quite accurate so I would like my learned friend Mr. Withopf to confirm to me that he said that on account of jurisdiction, we are talking about the applicability of Article 7(3) in "internal conflicts," because the interpretation I got was in "international conflicts." Did I understand you correctly, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: What I said, Ms. Residovic, I said, "in a non-international armed conflict."

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. That's what I thought you meant, but the interpretation I got was somewhat different, so I want to avoid any misunderstanding. I would also like to thank our colleagues from the OTP for having clarified this matter entirely to you, Your Honour, including that which the Defence believes, but nevertheless, I would like to say a few words about what we actually think. When I say "we," I'm referring to all three Defence teams, because we have identical views with regard to this particular matter. First and foremost, we believe that the question of jurisdiction is of great importance for each and every one of our clients. Not only that, though; we think that the applicable law in non-international conflicts in relation to Article 7(3) is of general interest for this Tribunal and of general interest for the application of international humanitarian law. Therefore, it is our position that we should devote due and considerable attention to this matter, and at this point the Defence is working separately on looking into customary law with regard to this particular matter. In our motion, several legal issues were raised, and we will try to present existing law to the Trial Chamber, the law that was in force when the alleged crimes were committed. We believe that the Trial Chamber should rule, in a decision of their own, on an alternative possibility, namely: If the Trial Chamber believes -- or rather, if we decide to file a joint motion, because we are going to have identical views with regard to each and every one of the issues raised, then the Defence fully agrees that we have the same number of pages for preparing this material as the Prosecutor did, that is to say, 50 pages, if we decide on a joint motion of this nature. However, if we were to submit separate motions to the Trial Chamber, then we believe that compiling separate motions requires a few formal yet necessary pages, and therefore, we think that the Trial Chamber should rule that each and every one of the parties should compose a paper on 25 pages respectively, that is to say, a total of 75 pages. I think that you understand the position of the Defence. Therefore, it would be our request for your ruling to make it possible for us either to submit a joint motion of 50 pages or separate submissions with 25 pages respectively for each and every one of the accused, a total of 75. Within the time frame that we were considering in terms of compiling this motion and carrying out the necessary preparations, our proposal is that, if we were to work as hard as possible and to do our very best, to make it possible for us to have either 30 days after the indictment enters into legal force or a total of 60 days. Naturally, this deadline would go for the other party as well. Both parties would, after that, have the obligation to respond within 15 days. In respect of this particular matter, and for the above-mentioned reasons, we believe that it would be necessary to have an oral hearing. As we have already said, these are questions that not only of interest to these parties that are here in this case; these are general legal issues that this Tribunal is indeed interested in. As for an amicus curiae, my learned friend from the Prosecution, Mr. Withopf, presented one of the positions presented during our meeting yesterday. That was not our position, though. We did not think that we had to call upon the permanent members of the Security Council. That was one of the opinions presented. Our position, though, is that the Court should pursue its own decision, as it will do, and if the Court believes that they should avail themselves of their authority to call in an amicus curiae, we have full trust in this kind of a decision of the Trial Chamber. However, it is not for us, the parties, to make suggestions to this effect to the Trial Chamber as to whether they are going to call in an amicus curiae or not. Since you also referred to the Sarajevo collection, I think that the Prosecution gave us access to most documents, or rather, all documents from the Sarajevo collection, and also selected military maps, except for one, and I believe that they will make it available to us today. However, we believe that the Prosecutor is duty-bound in respect of this issue to check audio and video cassettes and to make accessible to the Defence that material which would have to do with the applicability of Rule 68 in relation to what you have just mentioned. So this is the position that we have with regard to these particular matters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The Trial Chamber will consider the submissions of the parties. The reason why some of these motions, especially the one dealing with jurisdiction, is still under consideration is that you will appreciate that Trial Chamber II is the only Trial Chamber which has been divided into three sections, without corresponding legal support teams, so it has been rather heavily weighted down with work while waiting for legal support to be appointed. But the situation has now improved, so the motions should -- the decisions on the motions should be moving much faster, as from next week especially. The matters raised regarding page limits, I think the Trial Chamber will give due consideration to what the parties have said, and we will be issuing a written decision in due course. It is important, though, to comply with the practice directions; otherwise, there would be no use for the Tribunal to issue practice directions if at each stage parties feel they cannot conform. On the oral hearings, during the pre-trial stage it is normally the practice of the Tribunal, or rather, the Trial Chambers, to have written submissions as much as possible because of the courtroom heavy schedule. We have only three courtrooms and we are now having a lot of trials. And when the Appeals Chamber is sitting, they also require a courtroom. So during the pre-trial stage, as much as possible, parties should comply with written submissions. And in fact, there is a ruling, I think in Brdjanin and Talic, where the Trial Chamber did say reasons should be given why written submissions are not sufficient by any party who is applying for an oral hearing. Otherwise it would be a waste of court time, when the written submissions are sufficiently argued, for the Trial Chamber to have oral hearings. The experience has been what the Prosecution has alluded to, that usually it's a repetition of what is already in writing. There is nothing actually to stop a party from including every possible point they would like the Trial Chamber to consider in their written submissions. And in any case, the written submissions, except in situations where they are confidential, they are always in the public domain so that people are able to follow the arguments of the parties and are able to follow the reasoning of the Trial Chamber once a written decision is given. It saves on a lot of court time. On the issue of whether or not amicus curiae should be requested, this is a matter which very much depends on how the Trial Chamber will see the options as submitted by the Defence, and there is nothing to stop the parties to submit, under every stage, as to what was discussed by the members of the Security Council at the relevant time, on the relevant issues, or indeed any other body of the United Nations, to bring the matters to the attention of the Trial Chamber; otherwise, the Trial Chamber would be in a position to decide on this one. On the Rule 68 and the Sarajevo collection and the video and the other evidence which is not in paper form, I'm sure the Prosecution, in keeping with the provisions of Rule 68 and according to the submissions of the Defence, are in agreement that they have this obligation. And on this one, I think there will be a time limit for the Prosecution's obligations under Rule 66(A)(ii), and the Trial Chamber is of the view that we may be issuing an order in May of this year. On the motion regarding co-counsel, the assignment of co-counsel, the Trial Chamber is issuing a decision. I think latest by Tuesday next week, a decision should be there. But I'm of the view that this shouldn't hold the pre-trial stage at all, because we comply with what is in position as of now and that the co-counsel is on the case. On the submissions that -- the motion on jurisdiction, which has to be decided by the Trial Chamber, that a lot hinges on this as to what steps the Prosecution have to take in the preparation of the case, that has been noted, and as I explained earlier, the Trial Chamber is now having sufficient staff, so it should be able to decide very soon. I also note that in situations where the accused are on provisional release, there is a tendency sometimes not to comply with the Rules on pre-trial stage. I wish to point out that it is important to comply with the Rules on time limits with a pre-trial stage, because even though it appears as of now that all Trial Chambers are having trials, some of the trials may be shortened and the Trial Chamber may be available for the trial to start. So in my view, it isn't a good practice to keep stretching the time limits and also to keep stretching the pre-trial stage unnecessarily too long. It's obvious that it costs the Tribunal a lot of money for every sitting, and a lot of -- and for every sitting and every stage that the parties take. On the issue of the trial date, that is a matter that will be decided by the Trial Chamber once the motions have been decided and the major steps in the preparation have been complied with. We may be looking perhaps towards the end of this year, because from the records of the Trial Chamber, some cases may be coming to an end; the trials may be completed. Otherwise we may be looking at early next year. I'm aware that in the order on provisional release, there is an aspect of the accused reporting to the Tribunal some 60 days, I think, before the date of trial. I don't think that should be a problem, because the Trial Chamber can always change the days when the accused should report before the trial date. And in any case, it may not necessarily be Trial Chamber II which will take this trial. Any other Trial Chamber which may be ready can take the trial, and it will be up to that Trial Chamber to discuss with the parties as to when the trial can start. Although the discussion on pages seems to have been quite a matter with which the parties are concerned, I don't think I would like to give the number of pages right away. I would leave it and discuss it with the Trial Chamber, since the motions are under discussion, and see how best to deal with this, how many pages each party should have. In the event that it is a joint submission by the Defence or in the event that it is a separate submission, the Trial Chamber is very much aware that although it is going to be a joint trial, each accused person has his rights which must be complied with and which must be considered separately as much as possible. So the Trial Chamber will be very much aware that whatever decision we come up with does not undermine the rights of any of the accused to fully debate their case. There is another point on making it -- asking the parties to make it possible to have a list of agreed facts. I think that again can only be seriously debated once the decision on the motion has been issued by the Trial Chamber. I don't see any other matters that are remaining except if the Prosecution wishes to raise any matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Just one issue, Your Honour, just for clarification. You just mentioned that you will, with regard to Rule 66(A)(ii) issue an order in May. Does that mean the time limit is in May or does it mean the order will be issued in May, indicating a time limit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The order will be issued perhaps for the time limit to start running as from May.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Since there's one facet to be considered regarding the Rule 66(A)(ii) disclosure, and that's the issue that we also have to provide to disclose the Defence previous prior statements of our witnesses we want to use. The system-wide searches have been initiated. However, they have been put on hold. We only resume end of April. The results can only being expected at the end of May. Obviously there has to be an examination to be made that would cause some delay, a few weeks' delay. Realistically, we would only be in a position to disclose prior statements around end of June, beginning of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. Yes, that will be taken into consideration. Any other matters the Defence wishes to raise during this Status Conference? Yes?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, first of all I would like to thank you for stating in public that our clients are complying fully with all the Court orders in accordance with the decision on their provisional release. And secondly, I would like to say that we are looking through public documents in three trials, and these are voluminous materials. The Registry is providing significant support, but we are all in different locations, and we appreciate the Court's understanding in view of the fact that we cannot prepare so fast. So the dates that Your Honour has stated for the beginning of the trial are realistic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. That is noted. The Trial Chamber appreciates the cooperation that is being demonstrated by the parties to this case inasmuch as the discussions with the Senior Legal Officer show. I'm sure that everybody's doing their level best so that the pre-trial stage can be completed as soon as possible. The Trial Chamber, on its part, will deal with the matters that are before it as soon as possible so that the stages are not -- the pre-trial stages are not delayed. So I take it there are no other matters that the parties wish to raise, and we shall adjourn the Status Conference at this time until next time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: at 3.33 p.m.
